node.title: Re: /ee -> Use of uninitialized value in substitution iterator (without back references)
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
As per [doc://perlop#Regexp-Quote-Like-Operators], /ee means "Evaluate the right side as a string then eval the result." and "A /e will cause the replacement portion to be treated as a full-fledged Perl expression and evaluated right then and there. It is, however, syntax checked at compile-time. A second e modifier will cause the replacement portion to be evaled before being run as a Perl expression."

So basically, "$rhs" becomes qqq, which when [doc://eval]ed causes an error: Try adding print $@ to your code and you'll see Bareword "qqq" not allowed while "strict subs" in use at (eval 1) line 1., so [doc://eval] is returning undef which is causing the Use of uninitialized value in substitution iterator.

Running perl -e 'print eval("qqq");' prints qqq.

That's because that's not using [doc://strict] - perl -wMstrict -e 'print eval("qqq"); print $@;' prints Bareword "qqq" not allowed while "strict subs" in use at (eval 1) line 1.

And of course there's no warning with just /e instead of /ee; in the real program, I need /ee.

Perhaps your example is a little too abstracted from the original program? Needing /ee is somewhat rare in my experience. Could you show a more representative example of why you (think you) need it, perhaps we can come up with a better solution?
